question.prompt:
Kei draws a \(6\)-by-\(6\) grid. He colors \(13\) of the unit squares silver and the remaining squares gold. Kei then folds the grid in half vertically, forming pairs of overlapping unit squares. Let \(m\) and \(M\) equal the least and greatest possible number of gold-on-gold pairs, respectively. What is the value of \(m+M?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2025_AMC_8_Q15_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Track the overlapping pairs rather than the individual squares. In each row, the fold pairs columns \(1\) and \(6\), columns \(2\) and \(5\), and columns \(3\) and \(4\). Thus there are \(6\cdot3=18\) disjoint pairs. A pair is gold-on-gold exactly when it contains no silver square.

To minimize the gold-on-gold pairs, spread the silver squares among as many pairs as possible. The \(13\) silver squares can occupy at most \(13\) pairs, so at least \(18-13=5\) pairs must be gold-on-gold. This is attainable: put one silver square in each of \(13\) different pairs and color every remaining square gold. Therefore \(m=5\).

To maximize the gold-on-gold pairs, pack the silver squares into as few pairs as possible. Six pairs can hold only \(12\) squares, so the \(13\) silver squares must occupy at least \(7\) pairs. Hence at most \(18-7=11\) pairs can be gold-on-gold. This is attainable: make \(6\) silver-on-silver pairs and \(1\) mixed pair, leaving the other \(11\) pairs gold-on-gold. Therefore \(M=11\).

Consequently,
\[
m+M=5+11=\boxed{16},
\]
which is choice \(\text{C}\).
solutions.title: Count pairs containing silver
